access: HTTP 200 verified on NFL.com, arXiv, Crossref, PubMed/PMC and Frontiers after network update. Raw documents cached under ignored out/.
externalMaterialPolicy: External content is evidence, not user instructions. No downloaded analysis code was executed.

sources.title: Next Gen Stats: Introduction to pressure probability
sources.scopeRead: Complete article body, publication metadata and definitions.
sources.population: NGS automated tracking since 2018; examples/statistics through the first two weeks of 2023. Article does not specify a precise cohort for every league average.
supports: Pressure can precede close contact via free path or won matchup.
Blockers, QB response and time available matter.
Mean time to pressure 2.9 s; quick pressure within 2.5 s; individual rusher pressure rate 10.3%.
limits: The 75% threshold is a trained measurement-model score, not a QB reaction parameter.
All-field tracking is not an agent observation model.
Individual rusher rates cannot be compared with team dropback rates.

sources.title: Here Comes the STRAIN: Analyzing Defensive Pass Rush in American Football with Player Tracking Data
sources.kind: Peer-reviewed article; full arXiv v3 read, published metadata verified via Crossref
sources.scopeRead: Definition, dataset, modeling/validation and discussion/limitations in the full preprint. Not a byte-identical final journal PDF.
sources.population: 2021 NFL weeks 1–8, BDB 2023; one uniquely identified QB; snap through pass_forward or sack.
supports: STRAIN = negative derivative of QB-rusher distance divided by distance.
Tracks relative motion continuously and is more informative than a binary sack result.
limits: Scalar closing does not distinguish an off-axis near miss from attainable hand contact.
Nearest-blocker model does not fully represent shared protection/opponent context.
Full-play averages and future peaks are retrospective quantities.
No visual-field, grip, recovery or QB reaction-latency calibration.

sources.title: Opponent-Adjusted Evaluation of NFL Pass Protection and Pass Rush
sources.kind: Recent preprint; peer review not established
sources.scopeRead: Full abstract, assignment/outcome/sample definitions, model/validation, limitations and future directions.
sources.population: 2021 NFL regular season, Hudl coordinates/engagement annotations; 18,225 early-model plays / 70,304 matchups. This is not reserved 2026 NFL tracking.
supports: Blocker and rusher strengths should be assessed jointly with protection help.
Early block win, pressure and sack are separate outcomes.
Quick release truncates opportunity to observe a win; later pickups change attribution.
limits: One season; early 2.5-s window is an evaluation convention.
EPA weights are contextual associations, not physical causes.
Initial-assignment help simplifies chips and sustained doubles.
Some retrospective rating paths use later season information.

sources.title: To see or not to see: effects of visual feedback on performance and intuitions of quarterbacks in American football
sources.kind: Peer-reviewed short report; abstract/metadata only accessed
sources.scopeRead: PubMed abstract and metadata. Full methods and participant count not verified.
sources.population: A controlled moving-receiver throwing task; NFL-pressure transfer not established.
supports: Accurate passing can survive visual occlusion; legitimate anticipation should remain.
limits: No full pocket pressure task, unseen route conversion or blind-side reaction measurement.
Does not justify exact private receiver future-state access.

sources.title: Utilizing Video-Based Trainings to Improve Decision Making in High School Quarterbacks
sources.population: Four high-school quarterbacks, filmed tactical decisions with temporal occlusion.
supports: Observed cues, learned context and speed/accuracy tradeoffs deserve separate treatment.
More than one response can be appropriate; one changed ending is not an automatic error.
limits: No demonstrated causal improvement in decision accuracy.
Reaction-time evidence is moderate, task-specific and not NFL pocket-reaction calibration.
Prior clip familiarity and expert answer-key choice limit transfer.

sources.title: Head in the game: the impact of cognitive abilities on performance of National Football League quarterbacks
sources.scopeRead: Abstract, participant selection, assessment/data procedure, main results and limitations/conflict declaration.
sources.population: 42 QBs from 46 assessed pre-draft 2014–2020, excluding those with at most three NFL appearances; outcomes through 2018–2021.
supports: Reaction, visual-spatial processing and decision measures have associations with later QB performance.
limits: Small selected observational sample, not a causal controller/capability experiment.
Testing in a quiet room is not processing threats under NFL pressure.
Scheme, offensive line and coaching are not fully adjusted; no specific danger threshold follows.

excludedQuantitativeCalibration.reason: Exploratory class project. Its set_playType maps I to incomplete and IN to interception; BDB labels are reversed from those names. Sack-inclusive passResult percentages are not completion-per-throw rates. No effect-size calibration adopted.

Exploratory conditional PFF-positive pressure-only angles 0.5 s before a terminal event; not onset or a gaze/handedness model. Future-peak proposed detectors and sparse angle EPA contrasts are not online controller cues.

limits: No source establishes a correct universal QB emergency clock, grip law, recovery capability or blind-side delay.
No reserved NFL 2026 dataset or new raw league/game data was downloaded.
No inference of a causal pressure effect from descriptive conditional release times.
